beats.text: Writing a payroll program is easy. The rules are known, so you simply code them.
But what are the rules for recognising speech? People do it every day, and nobody can explain how.
So we let the computer learn from examples. Machine learning optimises a performance criterion, using example data or past experience.
What it learns is a model: a useful approximation, not the perfect truth.
The first kind of learning has a teacher. Every example comes with the right answer. That is supervised learning.
A bank knows each customer's income and savings, and whether they were low risk or high risk. Learning finds the thresholds that separate them. The answer is a class, so this is classification.
Now predict a used car's price from its mileage. The answer is a number, so this is regression. Learning finds the line.
Take the answers away. Only the inputs are left. That is unsupervised learning.
The learner can still find groups of similar examples, like customer segments. These groups are clusters, not classes. Nobody has named them.
The third kind is reinforcement learning. A robot in a maze gets no answer for each step. It gets a reward only at the end.
From that delayed reward, it learns a policy: which move to make, in every place.
Week one also finds associations. Of ten baskets with a computer, seven also hold a mouse. So the probability of a mouse, given a computer, is zero point seven.
One last idea. Some learners fix the form of the answer before they see any data. They are parametric.
The line, y equals w x plus w zero, is parametric. Its shape is chosen in advance. Learning only fills in w and w zero. More data never changes the form.
A nonparametric learner has no such fixed formula. A decision tree's questions, and how deep it grows, come from the data itself.
For the exam.
Supervised: every example has its answer.
Classification gives a class. Regression gives a number.
Unsupervised finds clusters, without labels.
Reinforcement learns a policy from a delayed reward.
Parametric fixes the form. Nonparametric does not.
